steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an empirical paper comparing Decision Transformer, CQL and behavior cloning for offline RL, asking when each one should be preferred.

    - 4.4 noise as random actions; simulates lots of exploration
  - Section 4.5 task complexity: state space dimensionality, task horizon
  - Section 4.6 stochastic environments: stochasticity x data quality
  - Section 4.7 using DT in practice: architecture (Appendix A), hyperparameters, scaling model size + data on atari

  - (1) DT more robust than CQL but needs more data
  - (2) DT best for sparse reward, low-quality data
  - (3) DT and BC preferable with longer horizon or suboptimal human demonstrators
  - (4) CQL best with high stochasticity + low data quality
  - (5) larger DT needs less training; more data improves atari scores

  - one study: theoretical conditions (near-deterministic dynamics, known conditioning function) favouring Sequence Modeling ("RCSL"); we add empirical insights
  - another: when Q-Learning beats Imitation Learning; we add DT / Sequence Modeling, training dynamics, learned policies

  - help choose an offline RL algorithm; practical guidance throughout
  - code and data: https://github.com/facebookresearch/rl_paradigm

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) tries to use existing datasets of agent behavior in an environment to produce effective policies. A key open question is which learning method should be preferred for offline RL. In this paper we investigate this question empirically. There are many offline RL algorithms, but we focus on three that have been studied a lot and so are relatively easy to interpret and compare: Conservative Q-Learning (CQL), Behavior Cloning (BC), and Decision Transformer (DT). CQL is from the class of Q-Learning and it uses temporal difference (TD) updates to learn a value function by bootstrapping. In theory it can learn effective policies even from very suboptimal trajectories in stochastic environments, but in practice it is unstable and sensitive to hyperparameters in the offline setting. BC is from the family of Imitation Learning and it mimics the behavior policy of the data, but it relies on the data being high-quality. DT is from the class of Sequence Modeling, which is a recently popularized paradigm that tries to transfer the success of Transformers into offline RL, but DT has been shown to struggle with stochastic dynamics.

We design targeted experiments to understand how the three algorithms perform when we vary properties of the data, the task, and the environment. We run the experiments on the commonly used d4rl, robomimic, and atari benchmarks. Table 1 gives a high-level summary of our key findings. In Section 4.1 we first establish baseline results on our benchmark tasks for CQL, BC, and DT, for dense-reward and sparse-reward settings. Then we run experiments to answer several key questions, and these are the core contributions of the paper:

- (Sections 4.2, 4.3, 4.4) How are agents affected when there is suboptimal data? Suboptimality can mean many things in offline RL, so we look at three definitions:
  - (Section 4.2) First we vary the amount of data the agents are trained on. We sort the trajectories in the dataset by their returns and give the agents either the best X% or the worst X% of the data, for different values of X. This lets us study sample efficiency when learning from high-quality and low-quality data.
  - (Section 4.3) Second, we study the impact of suboptimality that comes from longer trajectories in the dataset. In longer trajectories the rewarding states are usually further away from the early states, and this can affect the training dynamics.
  - (Section 4.4) Third, we look at the impact of adding noise to the data, in the form of random actions. This setting can be seen as simulating a common practical situation where the offline dataset came with a lot of exploration.

- (Section 4.5) How do agents perform when the task gets more complex? Here we study the impact of both state space dimensionality and task horizon on agent performance.

- (Section 4.6) How do agents perform in stochastic environments? Here we evaluate agent performance as we vary the degree of stochasticity and the data quality.

- (Section 4.7) How can DT be used effectively in practice? Since DT is strong overall in our findings, we give guidance on architecture (Appendix A) and hyperparameters for DT and we do a detailed analysis of scaling the model size and the amount of data in atari.

- Findings
  - (1) DT more robust than CQL, needs more data; (2) DT best for sparse reward / low-quality data
  - (3) DT and BC better with longer horizon or suboptimal human demonstrators; (4) CQL best with high stochasticity + low data quality
  - (5) larger DT needs less training; more data improves atari scores
- Prior work
  - one study: theoretical conditions (near-deterministic dynamics, known conditioning function) favouring Sequence Modeling ("RCSL"); we add empirical insights
  - another: when Q-Learning beats Imitation Learning; we add DT
- Takeaway
  - practical guidance on choosing an algorithm; code and data: https://github.com/facebookresearch/rl_paradigm

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) tries to use existing datasets of agent behavior in an environment to produce effective policies. A key open question is which learning method should be preferred for offline RL. In this paper we investigate this question empirically. There are many offline RL algorithms, but we focus on three that have been studied a lot and so are relatively easy to interpret and compare: Conservative Q-Learning (CQL), Behavior Cloning (BC), and Decision Transformer (DT). CQL is from the class of Q-Learning and it uses temporal difference (TD) updates to learn a value function by bootstrapping. In theory it can learn effective policies even from very suboptimal trajectories in stochastic environments, but in practice it is unstable and sensitive to hyperparameters in the offline setting. BC is from the family of Imitation Learning and it mimics the behavior policy of the data, but it relies on the data being high-quality. DT is from the class of Sequence Modeling, which is a recently popularized paradigm that tries to transfer the success of Transformers into offline RL, but DT has been shown to struggle with stochastic dynamics.

We design targeted experiments to understand how the three algorithms perform when we vary properties of the data, the task, and the environment. We run the experiments on the commonly used d4rl, robomimic, and atari benchmarks. Table 1 gives a high-level summary of our key findings. In Section 4.1 we first establish baseline results on our benchmark tasks for CQL, BC, and DT, for dense-reward and sparse-reward settings. Then we run experiments to answer several key questions, and these are the core contributions of the paper:

- (Sections 4.2, 4.3, 4.4) How are agents affected when there is suboptimal data? Suboptimality can mean many things in offline RL, so we look at three definitions:
  - (Section 4.2) First we vary the amount of data the agents are trained on. We sort the trajectories in the dataset by their returns and give the agents either the best X% or the worst X% of the data, for different values of X. This lets us study sample efficiency when learning from high-quality and low-quality data.
  - (Section 4.3) Second, we study the impact of suboptimality that comes from longer trajectories in the dataset. In longer trajectories the rewarding states are usually further away from the early states, and this can affect the training dynamics.
  - (Section 4.4) Third, we look at the impact of adding noise to the data, in the form of random actions. This setting can be seen as simulating a common practical situation where the offline dataset came with a lot of exploration.

- (Section 4.5) How do agents perform when the task gets more complex? Here we study the impact of both state space dimensionality and task horizon on agent performance.

- (Section 4.6) How do agents perform in stochastic environments? Here we evaluate agent performance as we vary the degree of stochasticity and the data quality.

- (Section 4.7) How can DT be used effectively in practice? Since DT is strong overall in our findings, we give guidance on architecture (Appendix A) and hyperparameters for DT and we do a detailed analysis of scaling the model size and the amount of data in atari.

Our key findings are: (1) DT is more robust than CQL but it also needs more data; (2) DT is the best choice in sparse-reward and low-quality data settings; (3) DT and BC are preferable when the task horizon increases, or when the data comes from suboptimal human demonstrators; (4) CQL is best in situations with both high stochasticity and low data quality; (5) larger DT models need less training, and scaling the amount of data improves scores on atari.

Our work fits a recent research trend that looks at the trade-offs between different algorithms for offline RL. One prior work outlined theoretical conditions, like nearly deterministic dynamics and prior knowledge of the conditioning function, under which Sequence Modeling (which they call "RCSL") is preferable. Our paper extends this research by asking carefully designed questions aimed at giving new empirical insights. Another prior work looked at when Q-Learning might be preferred over Imitation Learning. We expand on this by including the recently popularized DT as part of the Sequence Modeling paradigm, which gives insight into the training dynamics and learned policies of each algorithm.

We hope this paper helps researchers decide which offline RL algorithm to use in their application. All through the paper we give practical guidance on which algorithm is preferred, given the characteristics of the application. Code and data: https://github.com/facebookresearch/rl_paradigm.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) [1,2,3] aims to leverage existing datasets of agent behavior in an environment to produce effective policies. A key open question is: which learning method is preferred for offline RL? In this paper, we investigate this question empirically. Among many offline RL algorithms, we focus on three that have been studied extensively and are thus relatively easy to interpret and compare: Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) [4], Behavior Cloning (BC) [5], and Decision Transformer (DT) [6]. CQL, from the class of Q-Learning [7], uses temporal difference (TD) updates to learn a value function through bootstrapping. In theory, it can learn effective policies even from highly suboptimal trajectories in stochastic environments, but in practice it suffers from instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters in the offline setting [8]. BC, from the family of Imitation Learning [9], mimics the behavior policy of the data, but relies on the data being high-quality. DT, from the class of Sequence Modeling, is a recently popularized paradigm that aims to transfer the success of Transformers [10] into offline RL [6,11], yet it has been shown to struggle with stochastic dynamics [8].

We design targeted experiments to understand how these three algorithms perform as we vary properties of the data, task, and environment. Our experiments are conducted across the commonly used d4rl, robomimic, and atari benchmarks, and Table 1 shows a high-level summary of our key findings. In Section 4.1, we begin by establishing baseline results in our benchmark tasks for CQL, BC, and DT, for both dense-reward and sparse-reward settings. We then perform experiments to answer several key questions, which form the core contributions of this paper:

- • (Sections 4.2, 4.3, 4.4) How are agents affected by the presence of suboptimal data? As suboptimality can take on many meanings in offline RL, we consider three definitions:
  - – (Section 4.2) Our first setting varies the amount of data the agents are trained on. We sort trajectories in the dataset by their returns and expose the agents to either the best X% or the worst X% of the data for varying values of X. This lets us study sample efficiency when learning from high-quality and low-quality data.
  - – (Section 4.3) In our second experiment, we study the impact of suboptimality arising from longer trajectories in the dataset. In longer trajectories, rewarding states are typically further away from early states, which can impact training dynamics.
  - – (Section 4.4) Finally, in our third experiment, we examine the impact of adding noise to the data, in the form of random actions. This setting can be seen as simulating a common practical situation where the offline dataset was accompanied by a lot of exploration.

- • (Section 4.5) How do agents perform when task complexity is increased? To understand this, we study the impact of both state space dimensionality and task horizon on agent performance.

- • (Section 4.6) How do agents perform in stochastic environments? To investigate this, we evaluate agent performance as we vary the degree of stochasticity and data quality.

- • (Section 4.7) How can one effectively use DT in practice? Based on the overall strength of DT in our findings, we provide guidance on architecture (Appendix A) and hyperparameters for DT and perform a detailed analysis of scaling the model size and amount of data in atari.

Our key findings are: (1) DT is more robust than CQL but also requires more data; (2) DT is the best choice in sparse-reward and low-quality data settings; (3) DT and BC are preferable as the task horizon increases, or when data is obtained from suboptimal human demonstrators; (4) CQL excels in situations combining high stochasticity and low data quality; (5) larger DT models require less training, and scaling the amount of data improves scores on atari.

Our work aligns with a recent research trend examining the trade-offs among various algorithms for offline RL. [8] outlined theoretical conditions, such as nearly deterministic dynamics and prior knowledge of the conditioning function, under which Sequence Modeling (called "RCSL" in their work) is preferable. Our paper extends their research by asking carefully designed questions that provide novel empirical insights. [12] investigated when Q-Learning might be favored over Imitation Learning. Our research expands on this by incorporating the recently popularized DT as part of the Sequence Modeling paradigm, providing insight into the training dynamics and learned policies of each algorithm.

We hope this paper helps researchers determine which offline RL algorithm to use in their application. Throughout the paper, we provide practical guidance on which algorithm is preferred given the characteristics of the application. Code and data: https://github.com/facebookresearch/rl_paradigm.
